name: David Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, David. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. What you say is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Could you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at the potash mine at Elkhorn, a kilometre underground. It's a machine with a big spinning drum on the front that cuts the potash out of the wall, and it drops it onto a conveyor behind me. Potash is the pink salt they make fertiliser from, so I like to say I help grow everyone's bread.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a shift like, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We go down in the cage at six-thirty, travel twenty minutes to the panel, which is the area we're mining, and I cut until lunch. I eat with the young ones mostly, and I end up teaching them things, how to listen to the drum, how the roof sounds before it gives trouble. The cold and the salt on everything wear on you. My knees are older than me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a man's work still counts for something. I'd say it at the mosque after Friday prayers, where the brothers always ask about the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I can work to sixty-three, as Samira and I planned, and help our youngest, Yusuf, through his carpentry apprenticeship. That's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep cutting, keep teaching the young ones, keep our savings in the bank. I might use that chatbot thing a bit more, Yusuf showed me how, for writing letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Like a good meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What have you used the chatbot for so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used it to tidy up Yusuf's application for his apprenticeship, and to explain a letter from the tax office. It was clever enough. I still read everything twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the automation like underground at Elkhorn right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a trial machine on the other panel that cuts on a programme, with a man watching from a cabin. It cuts straight, but it doesn't hear the roof. Not yet, anyway.

S0.say: I'd say good, a man's work still counts for something. I'd say it at the mosque after Friday prayers, where people always ask about the mine.
S0.think: Privately it means I can work to sixty-three as planned and help my youngest through his carpentry apprenticeship. That's enough for me.
S0.do: Keeps cutting, teaching younger workers and saving in the bank as now. Uses a chatbot a little more for letters, as his son showed him.
S0.feel: Content, like after a good meal.
S0.quote: It cuts straight, but it doesn't hear the roof. Not yet, anyway.
S0.fieldNote: David takes pride in skills that are hard to put on paper, like listening for roof trouble. He uses AI for practical letters and double-checks everything. His mosque community and his youngest son's apprenticeship anchor his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has a right to modernise, but it should train its own people first, not hire strangers to watch screens. I'd say that to the shift boss directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the cutting machines go automatic within a few years here, because the trial already works on a straight panel. Someone has to watch them, and I'd like it to be me, once I've seen the others manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first lot of operators had done the remote course, ask them honestly how it went, then put my name down. We'd save a bit more, maybe two hundred a month, and Samira would keep her canteen hours. I'd also ask the training office whether I could help with apprentices part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. I've seen changes before, the old miners went when the continuous miners came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to go first. What if the seats are gone by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have waited too long, that's true. But I've also seen men rush into a new thing and look foolish. I'd keep my ear to the ground and move when the others say it's sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apprentices in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from an old Scottish fellow named Malcolm who taught me to listen to the roof. If the machines take the cutting, someone still has to pass on what a mine is. I'd feel useful doing that.

S1.say: I'd say the company has a right to modernise, but it should train its own people first rather than hire strangers to watch screens. I'd say it to the shift boss directly.
S1.think: Privately I think the cutting machines go automatic here within a few years because the trial already works. Someone has to watch them, and I'd like it to be me once I've seen others manage it.
S1.do: Waits until the first group finishes the remote course, asks how it went, then applies. Saves about two hundred more a month, keeps his wife's canteen income and asks the training office about part-time apprentice work.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, having lived through an earlier change of machines.
S1.quote: I've also seen men rush into a new thing and look foolish.
S1.fieldNote: David accepts the company's right to modernise but insists on loyalty to its own workers, which fits his outlook. He knowingly risks waiting too long, preferring proof. His wish to train apprentices comes from a mentor he still names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much, too fast, and families will have to carry each other. I wouldn't call for handouts, but I'd say the companies owe their people a decent send-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years puts me at sixty, three years short. If the machines can do even the listening, then my one special thing is gone. Four months of savings and Samira's canteen job won't carry us three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That week we'd stop sending extra money to my brother overseas, which hurts, and put the car upgrade off. I'd take redundancy if offered and look for work driving or doing maintenance at the mosque or the school. Our eldest, Omar, is a welder, and he'd want to help us, and I'd let him, which isn't easy for a father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf, halfway through his carpentry apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that hurts most. I'd tell him to finish it, because a finished thing is worth more than a half one. But I'd be lying if I said I knew it would get him a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning take from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The waiting. My way is to watch others and then step in. With two years, there's no time to watch, you either jump blind or you get left. I've never been a man who jumps blind.

S2.say: I'd say this is too much too fast and families will have to carry each other. I wouldn't call for handouts, but I'd say companies owe their people a decent send-off.
S2.think: Privately two years leaves me three years short at sixty, and if machines can even hear the roof, my one special skill is gone. Four months of savings and my wife's canteen job won't carry us.
S2.do: Stops the extra money to his brother overseas and delays the car upgrade that week. Takes redundancy if offered, looks for driving or maintenance work at the mosque or school, and accepts help from his eldest son.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: I've never been a man who jumps blind.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year version takes away David's method of watching before acting, and with it his sense of being a sensible man. Accepting help from his son is hard for him as a father. His pain is sharpest for his youngest son's half-finished apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a man to make a plan if he starts now. I'd tell the young ones at lunch not to buy new trucks on finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, which is my plan. So I think I'd make it, as long as they keep the old hands until the end. I'd still worry about the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the first group had done the remote course and said it was sound, I'd take it, probably in year one. I'd save harder and pay off the car. And I'd push the company to keep apprentices coming, maybe as a trainer myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a worry with a shape to it. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then learn to fix the machines, not just build cabinets. Wood and robots, both. He's a clever boy, he'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the company on apprentices. How would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the superintendent, he's a decent man. I'm not a union man, but I'd put my name on a letter from the older workers. A business that stops training its own young ones is eating its seed corn.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan if you start now. I'd tell the young ones at lunch not to buy new trucks on finance.
S3.think: Privately five years gets me to sixty-three, my plan, as long as they keep older workers until the end. I'd still worry about the last year.
S3.do: Takes the remote course in the first year once colleagues confirm it's sound. Saves harder, pays off the car and pushes the company through a letter from older workers to keep training apprentices, offering himself as a trainer.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a worry that has a shape he can work with.
S3.quote: A business that stops training its own young ones is eating its seed corn.
S3.fieldNote: With five years David's wait-then-act style works again, and he has a plan that fits his retirement date. He'd act through a letter to management rather than a union, which fits his outlook. His advice to his son blends old trade and new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning from God and the market both. Families should use it to set their children up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd retire at sixty-three and be sixty-eight when it arrives. I'd have my garden and the grandchildren. My concern is the boys, Omar and Yusuf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-three as planned and take the remote course when it's proven, mostly for my knees. I'd help Yusuf pay for an extra course in robot maintenance after his apprenticeship. That's where I'd put our spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the boys, calm for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put towards Yusuf's extra course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever it costs, within reason, maybe a couple of thousand. That's what fathers are for. We'd skip a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture you'd want to say to the people in charge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the apprenticeships, and don't let young men sit idle. Idle hands are the worst thing for a town. Give them work, not just money.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning from God and the market both. Families should use it to set their children up.
S4.think: Privately I'd retire at sixty-three and be sixty-eight with my garden and grandchildren when it arrives. My concern is my two sons.
S4.do: Works to sixty-three as planned and takes the remote course once proven, mostly for his knees. Puts spare money, perhaps a couple of thousand, towards a robot maintenance course for his youngest son after his apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his sons and calm for himself.
S4.quote: Give them work, not just money.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years shifts David's concern entirely to his sons' futures, and he would spend savings on his youngest's extra training. His request to those in charge is about work and apprenticeships, not handouts. The extra time lets his careful style work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is companies keeping older workers on as trainers for the last few years, and the government backing apprenticeships properly. Let the old hands teach while they still can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. A man who goes down the mine every day knows what he's worth. Take that away and you have to give him something else to be proud of, not just a cheque.

headlineQuote: A man who goes down the mine every day knows what he's worth.
portrait: David Ibrahim is a 58-year-old continuous miner operator a kilometre underground at the potash mine at Elkhorn, who teaches the young workers at lunch and values the skill of listening to the roof. He is devout, family-focused and wary of handouts, and he waits to see others succeed before trying something new, including the chatbot his son showed him. He is calm on the plateau, uneasy under steady change, and alarmed if AGI arrives in two years and leaves no time for his careful approach. With five or ten years he plans to retrain once it's proven, push for apprenticeships and spend his savings on his youngest son's training.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would put him out of work at sixty, three years short of his plan, with no time to watch before acting.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping older workers on as trainers in their last years and the government properly backing apprenticeships.
